topics.title: 了: completed action and change of state
topics.summary: 了 is not a past tense. After a verb it marks one action as done and bounded (often with a counted object); at the end of a sentence it says the situation is new or has changed. Ask two questions: is this a single finished event, and is something different now? If the sentence only describes a habit, a state, or something that did not happen, there is no 了.

topics.title: 过: experience
topics.summary: 过 right after a verb says the action has happened at least once before now: it is life experience, not the story of one event. 我去过北京 = 'I have been to Beijing (so I know it)'. The experience is over and done, the negative is 没…过 (过 stays), and 了 is what you use to report a particular event. A second use, V过了, simply means a routine thing is already done.

topics.title: 着: ongoing state
topics.summary: 着 after a verb says a state is holding: the door is open, she has a coat on, a picture is hanging there. Think of a photo, not a video. 在 + verb is the video (someone is busy doing it); 了 is the moment of change. The same 'held state' idea explains V1着V2 (doing V2 while in state V1), Place + V着 + thing, and commands like 拿着 (keep holding it).

topics.title: 在 / 正在 / 呢: action in progress
topics.summary: 在 or 正在 before a verb, or 呢 at the end of the sentence, says the action is going on at the moment you are talking about. It is not a tense: the time word decides whether that moment is now, yesterday or tomorrow. The click: 在 + verb = in the middle of doing; 在 + place = located at. No 了, no 'to be', and no 在 with states like 知道 or 喜欢.

topics.title: 要…了 / 快…了 / 就要…了: about to happen
topics.summary: 要…了, 快…了, 快要…了 and 就要…了 all say that something is about to happen. The 了 at the very end of the sentence is part of the pattern: it marks the new situation that is arriving, not a finished action. The four are close in meaning; what you have to decide is whether there is a specific time word (then use 就要), whether a noun or number follows directly (then use 快), and whether the 了 belongs at all.

topics.title: 是…的: stressing when, where, how
topics.summary: 是…的 is for a past event that both speakers already know happened. It does not report the event; it picks out one detail of it: when, where, how, who did it, or what for. 是 goes right before that detail and 的 closes the verb phrase. If the event itself is the news, use 了. If you are only filling in a detail of something already known, use 是…的.

topics.title: 的 / 得 / 地
topics.summary: 的, 得 and 地 all sound like de, so you choose by position, not by sound. Look at what comes right after the gap: a noun takes 的 (describing a thing), a verb takes 地 (how the action is carried out), and when the gap follows a verb or adjective and what comes next comments on it (how well, to what extent, whether it can be done) you need 得.

topics.title: 的: when to use it and when to drop it
topics.summary: 的 links whatever describes a noun to that noun, and the describing part always comes first: owner, adjective phrase or a whole clause + 的 + noun. The idea that makes it click: 的 marks a loose, built-on-the-spot description. Tight, ready-made pairs (我妈妈, 好朋友, 三本书) do without it, and when the noun is obvious you can drop the noun and let 的 stand in for it (我的, 红的, 吃的).

topics.title: Result complements
topics.summary: A Chinese verb names only the attempt: 找 is 'look for', 看 is 'look', 听 is 'listen'. To say what came of it you glue a result word straight onto the verb: 找到 found, 看见 saw, 听懂 understood, 做完 finished. Verb + result behaves as one word: nothing goes between them, 了 and the object come after both, and 'it did not turn out' is 没.

topics.title: Directional complements
topics.summary: A direction word after a verb says where the action goes: 进来 come in, 拿出去 take out, 站起来 stand up. 来 means toward the speaker, 去 means away. The one idea: the verb says how, the complement says which way, and a place word must sit before 来/去 (回家去). The same endings also carry fixed extra meanings: 起来 start or judge, 下去 keep going, 下来 settle or record, 出来 figure out or produce, 上 attach or achieve.

topics.title: Potential complements: can / cannot manage
topics.summary: Put 得 or 不 between a verb and its result or direction to say whether the result can be reached: 看得懂 'can understand (by reading)', 看不懂 'cannot'. It is about being able to manage it, not about permission. When English says 'can't' and the reason is that you would fail (too hard, too far, too many, too expensive), Chinese uses Verb + 不 + Result, not 不能.

topics.title: Degree complements with 得
topics.summary: To say how well, how fast, how early an action is done, Chinese puts the comment after the verb: Verb + 得 + (很) adjective. The idea that makes it click: 得 must touch the verb. An object, 了 or 不 can never sit between them, so the object is moved out of the way and 不 goes after 得. The same 得 after an adjective adds 'extremely': 热得很, 累得要命.

topics.title: Duration and frequency
topics.summary: How long and how many times are complements: they go AFTER the verb (学了两年, 去过两次), while the time WHEN something happens goes before it. The one idea: the verb comes first, then the amount. The amount moves in front of the verb only when the action did not happen (两年没见).

topics.title: Core word order
topics.summary: Chinese sets the scene before the action: who, then when, where, with whom and how, and only then the verb and its object. Almost everything English puts after the verb (tomorrow, at home, with friends, by subway, also, already) goes before it in Chinese, and question words simply sit where the answer would sit.

topics.title: Coverbs (prepositions)
topics.summary: Chinese prepositions (coverbs) such as 在, 给, 跟, 对, 从, 离, 往, 用 set the scene for the action: where, with whom, to whom, from where, with what. The scene comes first, so the coverb phrase stands BEFORE the verb, not after it as in English. Only a place or person that the action ends up at (放在, 送到, 寄给) follows the verb.

topics.title: 把 construction
topics.summary: 把 pulls a known, specific object in front of the verb so the sentence can say what was done TO it: where it ended up, what state it is in now, who got it. So the verb can never stand bare after 把: something must follow it (a result, a direction, 了, 在/到/给 + destination, 一下). Think 'take X and do-something-to-completion'. No change to the object, no 把.

topics.title: 被 passive
topics.summary: 被 puts the thing affected first and the doer second: Receiver + 被 + doer + verb + what happened to it. The sentence is about the receiver and how it ended up, so the verb has to carry a result or 了, exactly as in a 把 sentence turned around. Chinese uses 被 far less than English uses 'was done': when a thing obviously cannot act by itself, the plain sentence (作业写完了) is already passive.

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.summary: Chinese compares with word order, not with endings like '-er'. The frame is A 比 B + adjective, and the adjective stays bare: how much more goes AFTER it (高一点儿, 高得多, 高三厘米), never 很 before it. 'Less than' is A 没有 B + adjective, 'the same' is A 跟 B 一样, and 更, 最, 比较 and 越来越 are adverbs that sit right before the adjective.

topics.title: 有 / 在 / 是 and existence sentences
topics.summary: Chinese picks the verb and the word order by whether the thing is new or already known. New, indefinite thing: start with the place and put the thing last (Place + 有 / V着 / V了 + a thing). Known, definite thing: put it first and locate it with 在. 是 after a place identifies what occupies it. A place is a noun plus a location word (桌子上), never an English-style preposition phrase.

topics.title: 连…都 / 也: even
topics.summary: 连 X 都/也 means 'even X': it picks the most extreme case and says the statement holds even there. 连 goes right before the thing that is surprising, that thing moves in front of the verb, and 都 or 也 must follow it. Think of 连 and 都/也 as two halves of a frame: X sits inside, and everything else (不, 没, the verb) comes after 都/也.

topics.title: 不 vs 没
topics.summary: 不 and 没 both mean 'not', but they answer different questions. 不 denies that something is so or will be so: habits, plans, willingness, qualities, states and modal verbs. 没(有) denies that something happened or has happened up to a point in time, and it is the only negative for 有. Ask yourself: 'isn't / won't / doesn't' (不) or 'didn't / hasn't' (没)?

topics.title: 会 / 能 / 可以
topics.summary: English 'can' and 'will' split three ways. 会 is know-how you learned, and also 'will' for a prediction. 能 is being able in practice: the situation, your body or your capacity lets it happen, often with an amount. 可以 is 'it is allowed' or 'that option is open'. Ask which meaning of 'can' you intend: learned it, able to right now, or allowed to.

topics.title: 就 vs 才
topics.summary: 就 and 才 are adverbs that add the speaker's attitude. 就 says something happened sooner, faster or more easily than expected; 才 says it happened later, slower or with more effort. Both sit after the subject and before the verb. The time or amount they comment on comes before them (八点就来了 / 八点才来). When a number comes after 才, it means 'only' (才三岁).

topics.title: 又 / 再 / 还
topics.summary: English 'again', 'still' and 'more' are split three ways. 又 looks back: the repeat has already happened, or is certain to come round. 再 looks forward: the repeat has not happened yet (requests, plans, 'first..., then...'). 还 means the situation goes on or something is added: still, also, and 'again' in questions and before 想 / 要. Ask 'has it happened yet?', then check where the modal verb is.

topics.title: 都 and 也
topics.summary: 都 (all, both) and 也 (also, too) are adverbs, so they sit after the subject and before the verb, never at the start or end of the sentence the way English 'too' and 'all of' do. 都 looks back: it totals something already said to its left. Get the slot right, put 也 before 都, and put both before 不/没, and most of this topic is solved.

topics.title: 二 vs 两
topics.summary: Both mean 'two'. 两 answers 'how many?': it stands in front of a measure word or a unit (两个人, 两天, 两点). 二 is the number itself: counting, digits, ordinals, dates, and every 二 inside a bigger number (十二, 二十). If you could put 'second' or read the figure out as a digit, use 二; if you are counting things, use 两.

topics.title: 还是 vs 或者
topics.summary: Chinese has two words for 'or'. 还是 asks the listener to pick one (which one?), so it lives in questions and in 'whether A or B' clauses. 或者 simply lists possibilities in a statement (either is fine). Ask yourself: is the choice still open and being asked about? Then 还是. 还是 also means 'still' and, with 吧, 'had better'.

topics.title: 一点儿 vs 有点儿
topics.summary: Both mean 'a bit', but they sit in different places and say different things. 有点儿 goes BEFORE an adjective or verb and reports how things are, usually a complaint: 有点儿贵 'a bit (too) expensive'. 一点儿 goes AFTER an adjective to mean 'a bit more' (便宜一点儿 'a bit cheaper') or BEFORE a noun to mean 'a little of' (一点儿水). 儿 is optional in writing (一点, 有点).

topics.summary: A particle at the very end of a sentence does not change what happened; it tells the listener how to take the sentence: a yes/no question (吗), 'and what about...?' or 'still going on' (呢), a suggestion or a guess (吧), warmth (啊), 'obviously' (嘛, 呗), 'I assure you' (的), 'things are different now' (了). topics.title: Question forms
topics.summary: Chinese never moves words to make a question. Keep statement order and mark the question exactly once: add 吗, or double the verb (去不去), or offer a choice with 还是, or put a question word in the slot where the answer will go. One sentence, one question marker; that single idea removes most errors.

topics.title: Measure words in sentences

topics.title: Separable verbs
topics.summary: Words like 见面, 睡觉, 结婚 and 帮忙 look like one verb but are really verb + object (见 'see' + 面 'face'). The object slot is already full, so no second object can follow, and everything that normally sits between a verb and its object (了, 过, a duration, a count, 完, 的-phrases) goes in the middle of the word. topics.title: Paired connectors
topics.summary: Chinese links two clauses with a matched pair: an opener in the first clause (因为, 如果, 不管, 只有) and a fixed partner in the second (所以, 就, 都, 才). Learn each opener together with its partner, and remember that the partners 就, 才, 都, 也, 还 are adverbs: they come after the second subject, never in front of it.

topics.title: Reduplication and V 一下
topics.summary: Doubling a verb (看看, 休息休息, 散散步) or adding 一下 makes the action short, casual or a try: 'have a look', 'take a little rest'. It only fits actions you can do briefly, so it cannot combine with anything that says ongoing, experienced, finished or how long. Doubling an adjective (大大的, 高高兴兴) makes it vivid and already carries its own degree, so 很 is never added.

topics.title: Numbers, dates, clock time and money in sentences
topics.summary: How numbers behave inside real sentences: dates, clock time, prices, ages, rough amounts and ordinals. The idea that makes it click: Chinese always goes from the biggest unit to the smallest (year, month, day, part of day, hour, minute), counts large numbers in 万 (ten thousands) rather than thousands, and gives every small word (多, 半, 左右, 第, 零) one fixed slot around the number and its measure word.

topics.title: Tone changes: 不, 一 and third tones
topics.summary: Some syllables change tone because of the tone that follows. 不 and 一 switch depending on the next syllable, a 3rd tone before another 3rd tone rises like a 2nd, and before any other tone it just stays low. Always look one syllable ahead. Pinyin here shows 不 and 一 as spoken (bú, yí, yì) but keeps the written 3rd-tone mark (nǐ hǎo, said ní hǎo).
